BOX 19.5  Research to Practice
Considerations for future research include an investigation
into the relationship between folate and/or B12 deﬁ ciency and 
iron deﬁ ciency, since they often appear together. Megalo-
blastic anemias increase the absorption of dietary iron from 
the GI tract, due to feedback mechanisms induced by faulty 
erythropoiesis, and often increase iron storage, ferritin levels,
and saturation levels of transferrin. Despite this phenom-
enon, spuriously low iron values may be recorded with the 
use of only hematocrit, hemoglobin, and other non-speciﬁ c, 
nonsensitive measures. These spurious ﬁ ndings may in fact
be due to rapid mobilization of iron for new erythropoiesis or 
some other mechanism involving rapid cell division. This may 
be due to abnormal vitamin A metabolism in iron deﬁ ciency, 
since hepatic retinol mobilization is adversely affected by 
iron deﬁ ciency and retinol is essential for erythropoiesis.1
Depending on the circumstances, various abnormalities in the 
RBC population may co-exist in patients with iron deﬁ ciency
and megaloblastic anemias of nutritional origin.2, 3
